title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Nepal’s recent developments reflect a mixed economic picture, with encouraging export performance and infrastructure progress alongside mounting challenges in tourism, agriculture and public spending. Strong growth in tea exports through Kakarbhitta, coupled with substantial earnings from large cardamom, highlights the potential of agricultural exports to strengthen foreign trade and support rural livelihoods. However, rising international prices of maize and soybean meal have increased livestock feed production costs by 15 percent, placing additional pressure on poultry farmers and potentially affecting consumer prices.

Tourism presents another area of concern, particularly in Koshi Province, where declining foreign arrivals and hotel occupancy indicate weakening demand despite considerable tourism potential. Similarly, Gandaki Province’s low budget utilisation, particularly in capital expenditure, raises questions about the timely implementation of development projects.

Meanwhile, the completion of the long-delayed Khajura road expansion demonstrates the importance of infrastructure investment in improving connectivity and commercial activity. Temporary transport disruptions caused by landslides, however, highlight Nepal’s vulnerability to natural hazards.

At the international level, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal’s emphasis on climate justice underscores Nepal’s need for stronger global climate financing and adaptation support. Overall, these developments point to the importance of improving public spending efficiency, strengthening export competitiveness, supporting vulnerable industries, promoting sustainable tourism and accelerating climate-resilient infrastructure development.

Climate adaptation is a matter of climate justice: Foreign Minister Khanal

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said that climate adaptation should not be viewed merely as a technical or environmental response but also as an issue of climate justice. Addressing the High-Level Dialogue on Adaptation organised by the Least Developed Countries (LDCs) on the sidelines of the ongoing United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP-31) in Antalya, Turkey, Khanal said that least developed countries, despite contributing the least to global climate change, are among the hardest hit by its increasingly severe impacts. “For the least developed countries, adaptation is not only a technical or environmental response; it is also a matter of climate justice. Although our contribution to climate change is minimal, we are bearing the brunt of its increasingly severe impacts,” he said. During his address, Khanal highlighted the human and economic losses Nepal has suffered from recent climate-induced disasters. He stressed that climate-vulnerable countries could no longer afford to delay urgent climate action.

Gold and silver investments generate annual returns amid regulatory changes in Nepal

Gold prices in Nepal recorded an annual increase of around 17 percent, rising from Rs 241,500 to Rs 284,300 per tola (11.66 grams). However, prices have declined from their record high of Rs 339,300 per tola, reached on January 29. Silver also registered an annual price gain of 25.77 percent, increasing from Rs 3,065 to Rs 3,855 per tola, despite falling from its peak of Rs 7,505. Market analysts attributed the stronger growth in domestic prices compared to international markets partly to the government’s decision to increase customs duties on gold and silver from 10 percent to 20 percent through the national budget. Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates also contributed to changes in local prices.

Nepali tea exports through Kakarbhitta nearly double

Nepali tea exports to India through the eastern border point of Kakarbhitta have increased significantly, with both export volume and earnings recording substantial growth in the first month of the current fiscal year compared to the corresponding period last year. According to data from the Mechi Customs Office, Nepal exported 1,715,932 kilograms of tea worth Rs 495.45 million during Asoj of the current fiscal year 2083/84 BS. In comparison, 924,445 kilograms of tea worth Rs 247.49 million were exported during the same month of the previous fiscal year 2082/83. This represents an increase of more than 85 percent in export volume, while export earnings have nearly doubled. Besides tea, cardamom and plywood also accounted for a significant share of exports through the Kakarbhitta border point. The Mechi Customs Office reported that cardamom worth Rs 988.88 million and plywood worth Rs 442.35 million were exported during Asoj.

Large cardamom exports through Kakarbhitta generate Rs 988.8 million

Nepal exported large cardamom worth Rs 988.8 million through the Kakarbhitta customs point between September 17 and October 17, according to the Mechi Customs Office. During the period, 541,940 kilograms of large cardamom were exported to India. Other major export items included 1,715,932 kilograms of tea valued at Rs 495.4 million, 118,444 kilograms of plywood worth Rs 442.3 million and 1,319,140 kilograms of broom grass valued at Rs 89.5 million. These products were sourced from eastern districts, including Jhapa, Ilam, Panchthar and Taplejung. Additional exports during the reporting period included 46,745 kilograms of chhurpi worth Rs 89.5 million, 2,080,763 kilograms of iron sheets valued at Rs 298.4 million and 48,318 kilograms of dried meat worth Rs 48.3 million.

Rising maize and soybean prices push livestock feed production costs up by 15 percent

Livestock feed production costs across Nepal have increased by approximately 15 percent following a rise in international prices of imported maize and soybean meal. According to industry figures, the price of Indian maize has climbed from Rs 36 to more than Rs 50 per kilogram. Similarly, soybean meal imported from the United States and Bangladesh has become more expensive, with prices increasing from Rs 87 to Rs 95 per kilogram. Bran prices have also risen from Rs 35 to Rs 47 per kilogram. In response to higher production costs, manufacturers have increased broiler feed prices by Rs 5 per kilogram and layer feed prices by Rs 4. Retail prices of livestock feed now range between Rs 55 and Rs 75 per kilogram. Industry stakeholders said the rising costs have also increased egg production expenses by Rs 2 to Rs 3 per egg. They warned that poultry farmers are facing mounting financial pressure due to higher prices of chicks, live chickens and animal feed, with some producers being forced to discontinue operations.

Foreign tourist arrivals and hotel occupancy decline in Koshi Province: NRB

Hotel occupancy in Koshi Province fell to an average of 32 percent in fiscal year 2025/26, down from 39.2 percent in the previous fiscal year, according to a regional economic study published by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). The study also recorded a 21.8 percent decline in foreign tourist arrivals at hotels across the province. This followed a growth of 28.6 percent in the preceding year. A total of 47,457 foreign visitors were recorded, with arrivals from India and other international markets declining, although Chinese visitor numbers registered a modest increase. Passenger traffic at regional airports also decreased by 4.9 percent to 1,217,381 during the review period. Despite the slowdown in tourism indicators, the services sector continues to play a significant role in the provincial economy, contributing 49.85 percent of Koshi’s gross domestic product (GDP). The report also highlighted the province’s considerable tourism potential, particularly in ecotourism, adventure tourism, mountaineering and religious pilgrimage.

Gandaki Province spends 8.15 percent of annual budget in first trimester

The Gandaki Province Government spent 8.15 percent of its annual budget during the first trimester of fiscal year 2026/27, ending October 17. According to provincial financial records, total expenditure reached Rs 2.692 billion against an annual budget allocation of Rs 32.999 billion. Of the Rs 12.723 billion allocated for recurrent expenditure, Rs 1.438 billion was spent, representing 11.3 percent of the allocation. Meanwhile, capital expenditure stood at Rs 1.253 billion, or 6.26 percent of the Rs 20.026 billion earmarked for development projects. Among the provincial ministries, the Ministry of Health recorded the highest budget utilisation rate, spending 11.5 percent of its total allocation of Rs 3.312 billion during the review period.

First hunting season of fiscal year begins at Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve

The first hunting season of fiscal year 2026/27 has begun at the Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve, with foreign hunters permitted to hunt 10 blue sheep (naur) and seven Himalayan tahr across designated hunting blocks. According to reserve officials, 11 foreign hunters have already arrived, while six more are expected to participate in the season, which runs from mid-September to mid-December. While international hunters are visiting designated high-altitude hunting areas, domestic tourists and nature enthusiasts have also been exploring the reserve’s valleys and alpine pastures, including Niseldhor, Bukipatan and Jaljala. During the previous fiscal year, hunting activities at the reserve resulted in 21 blue sheep and 11 Himalayan tahr trophies, generating Rs 41.7 million in government revenue. The reserve also attracted approximately 37,000 domestic and international visitors to the surrounding areas of Rukum East, Baglung and Myagdi districts during the previous fiscal year.

Landslide at Ghoptebhir causes major traffic congestion along Prithvi Highway

A dry landslide at Ghoptebhir in Ichchhakamana Rural Municipality-4 of Chitwan caused significant traffic congestion along the Narayangadh–Muglin section of the Prithvi Highway on Tuesday. Road maintenance crews and security personnel cleared the debris, allowing vehicles to resume movement along a single lane. However, heavy traffic, particularly due to increased travel during the Tihar festival, combined with narrow road sections and existing bottlenecks near bridges, resulted in long queues in both directions. Thousands of passengers travelling from Kathmandu to various destinations for the Tihar celebrations were stranded for several hours. Traffic police worked to manage vehicle movement and ease congestion along the affected highway section.

Four-lane road completed along Khajura market section of Postal Highway

Construction of a four-lane road along a 1,800-metre stretch of Khajura market on the Nepalgunj–Gulariya Postal Highway has been completed, bringing an end to a project that remained stalled for nine years. The project was initially awarded in 2017 under the Road Division. However, delays and complaints over substandard construction work led to the termination of the original contract. The Hulaki Highway Directorate subsequently took responsibility for the project and awarded a new contract worth Rs 70.1 million to Mattahawa–NAT–Starlight JV. The completed section features asphalt concrete paving across a 16-metre-wide roadway, along with two-metre-wide footpaths and bridge infrastructure. Local authorities said the upgraded road is expected to improve connectivity and facilitate commercial activities in the Khajura market area.

publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Vinayraj Pandey is known as a key figure in laying the foundation of modern Nepali cricket.

He spent more than five decades serving Nepali cricket. Joining the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) around 2022 BS, Pandey held positions from Treasurer, General Secretary, to President of CAN.

It was due to his administrative leadership and diplomatic initiatives that Nepal obtained Affiliate Membership and Associate Membership of the International Cricket Council (ICC). Furthermore, Nepal became a member of the Asian Cricket Council (ACC).

His contribution to the construction and expansion of the TU International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur is considered invaluable.

He is respected in the Nepali sports world as an outspoken individual, an expert in sports diplomacy, and a dedicated sports administrator.

At one time, with extreme lack of resources, clay pitches, and relying on a limited number of players, Nepali cricket embarked on its international journey, and today it has entered a new era.

The roaring crowds of thousands in the stadium, investments worth crores, participation of international-level players, and the ongoing third season of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) are proving the professional height of Nepali cricket to the world.

But how was the foundation of this grandeur and glamour that we see today laid? What struggles and vision brought Nepali cricket to this professional point? And how is the ongoing NPL impacting the future of Nepali cricket, the domestic structure, and the improvement of the national team's level?

title: Nepal Tourism Board CEO Selection Faces Scrutiny Amidst Allegations of Political Interference - Ratopati
description: Nepal Tourism Board CEO Selection Faces Scrutiny Amidst Allegations of Political Interference  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The tourism sector is in turmoil after a shortlist of 16 candidates was prepared from 42 applicants for the post of Nepal Tourism Board's Executive Chief. Amidst the general expectation that a qualified person will come to this institution, which has the main responsibility of promoting the country's tourism, various criticisms have started regarding the transparency and credibility of this process.

In this regard, the selection committee and the Public Service Commission, which have been given the responsibility of recommending the CEO appointment, are also being evaluated on how much they have maintained their institutional dignity and credibility. This selection process has also raised doubts about the impartial evaluation of the capabilities of qualified and experienced candidates.

Spirit of Partnership and Legal Basis

Established under the Nepal Tourism Board Act, 2053, this institution is a unique and autonomous body based on the cooperation between the government and the private sector. The main objective of the board is to earn foreign currency and create employment through tourism expansion while conserving natural and cultural heritage.

Section 9 of the Act ensures balanced representation of government officials and private sector businessmen on the Board of Directors. Its clear objective is to make the best use of professional experience, independent perspective, and expertise in the decision-making process.

However, looking at recent practices, it seems that the representation of the private sector has been reduced to mere formality, and attempts are being made to operate the board under party influence. Section 14(1) of the Act and Rules 8 and 9 of the Tourism Board Regulations, 2055, mandate a postgraduate degree and at least 10 years of experience in the tourism sector for the executive chief.

According to the right to equality guaranteed by Article 18 of the Constitution of Nepal, the selection of public posts should be based on objective, equal, and legal criteria, not arbitrarily.

Political Influence vs. Professional Impartiality

It is not uncommon for leadership in public bodies to change with changes in government. It can be considered natural for the government to seek capable and result-oriented leadership to effectively implement its policies and programs.

While it may not be unnatural for political leadership to want to promote individuals they trust, political proximity can never be a substitute for minimum legal qualifications and open competition.

Appointing individuals to public posts by prioritizing party affiliation over qualifications is a blatant mockery of the rule of law. Political trust and the professional capacity required to lead an institution are entirely different matters. When the merit system is discarded to fulfill political ambitions, the entire institutional structure collapses.

Selection of 16 People: Undervaluing Expertise and Experience?

The process adopted while making public the shortlist of 16 candidates out of 42 applications for the post of Board's Executive Chief has raised serious questions. High academic individuals who have been active in the tourism and civil aviation sector for a long time were in competition in this process.

It is surprising and suspicious that researchers like Dr. Lekhnath Bhandari, Dr. Gyanendra Ratna Tuladhar, and Dr. Suryabahadur Ghimire, who hold doctorates in tourism itself, were not even included in the preliminary shortlist of 16.

Furthermore, the fact that Gyaneshwor Prasad Singh Mahato, an experienced personality in the tourism sector who has previously been among the final three candidates for the executive chief selection, is not even among the 16 this time raises a big question mark on the impartiality of the selection process.

On what criteria were candidates with higher education, research, and decades of experience left behind? The selection committee's hesitation to publicly clarify the marks given to candidates' educational qualifications and expertise and the objective basis on which 16 people were selected fuels the suspicion that something is amiss.

Responsibility of the Selection Committee and Autonomy of the Private Sector

Ramkrishna Lamichhane, Director General of the Department of Tourism, and from the private sector, Pemba Sherpa and Sahadev Dhamala are involved in the executive chief selection process as administrative leaders.

While respecting the administrative and professional contributions of these individuals, it is natural for public questions to arise regarding the decision-making process they undertook. Those in public responsibility cannot evade accountability.

Representatives from the private sector should have been able to advocate for merit independently and fearlessly, instead of becoming passive shadows of government leadership. The very spirit of the Tourism Board was to protect the institution from political interference through the majority role of the private sector. However, if the selection committee itself has reached a decision under pressure or influence, it has tarnished the autonomy of the private sector and the dignity of the selection committee.

Neglect of Higher Education and Research

Years of dedication and investment are spent on research at the doctoral, MPhil, or postgraduate levels from prestigious educational institutions like Tribhuvan University. It is ironic that on one hand, the state adopts policies prioritizing higher education and research, while on the other hand, it throws away the qualifications of experts in the relevant field into the dustbin when selecting leadership for public institutions.

Certainly, academic degrees or certificates alone are not the sole standard for leadership capacity. Managerial skills, international relations, and strategic thinking are equally necessary to run an organization.

However, it is not justifiable to completely disregard subject matter knowledge and research, certified by degrees, without any objective reason. Such a tendency discourages skilled manpower needed for the nation.

Past Practice and Test for Current Leadership

My experience working as a former member of the Board of Directors of the Nepal Tourism Board suggests that method, capability, and institutional needs should be paramount in leadership selection.

At that time, when we selected Deepak Raj Joshi as the Executive Chief through open competition, Dr. Dhananjay Regmi succeeded in reaching the final three based on his high academic qualifications, experience, and work plan. Only through fair competition can suitable leadership be obtained.

In this context, the role of the line ministry, the Ministry of Culture, Tourism, and Civil Aviation, should be regulatory, not interventionist. For the current minister, Khadga Raj Paudel (Ganes), this process is also a trial by fire. The ministry must make the selection committee transparent to maintain institutional good governance without interfering in the board's autonomy. Saving the institution's credibility is the first duty of the minister and the government, rather than fulfilling the political ambition of recruiting their close associates.

Transparent Criteria Essential for Credibility

To make the selection process free from controversy, the committee must publicly disclose the marks for educational qualifications, experience, and work plans as stipulated in the Selection and Appointment Recommendation Procedure, 2083. Unless the details of who obtained how many marks in which category among all 42 applicants are publicly disclosed transparently, the suspicion surrounding this process will not be dispelled.

Candidates who were not shortlisted should be provided an environment to view the basis of their evaluation as per the Right to Information Act. Furthermore, the committee must be able to present clear grounds that there was no conflict of interest or external political pressure in the selection process.

The final stage of appointment requires a real test of knowledge of the national and international tourism market, leadership capacity, and visionary work plan, not just formality.

The Tourism Board is not a platform for fulfilling personal or party interests; it is a shared institution connected to the entire country's economy. At a time when there is opposition, portraying the board as an unproductive 'white elephant', the selection of its leadership must be fair, impartial, and based on merit.

Any selection that sidelines qualified and expert individuals at the initial stage cannot make the institution dynamic. Accepting the supremacy of law over individuals and adopting a transparent evaluation system is the only option to save the reputation of the Tourism Board.

title: Humanitarian action amidst global crises Hong Kong Red Cross sustains support in Gaza and Nepal - The Standard (HK)
description: Humanitarian action amidst global crises Hong Kong Red Cross sustains support in Gaza and Nepal  The Standard (HK)
publisher.title: The Standard (HK)
full_article:
In an era marked by frequent natural disasters and protracted armed conflicts, countless innocent lives face multifaceted threats, demanding global solidarity and immediate humanitarian intervention. The Hong Kong Red Cross (HKRC) recently hosted a media sharing session to bring critical attention to the enduring plight of communities in Gaza, marking three years since the escalation of the conflict, and to shed light on the devastating floods in Nepal. Featuring frontline staff and medical volunteers, the event highlighted their frontline experiences and underscored that communities affected by crises still urgently require continued humanitarian intervention.

ADVERTISEMENT SCROLL TO CONTINUE WITH CONTENT

Through the close coordination and joint efforts of its three core components, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement addresses global humanitarian crises: the ICRC, which specialises in humanitarian work in armed conflicts and war-torn areas to protect victims and promote international humanitarian law; IFRC, which coordinates disaster relief, emergency responses, and public health crises globally; and National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies across 191 countries, which act as auxiliaries to public authorities and actively mobilise resources, professional expertise, and medical volunteers to support international and regional relief operations.

The profound and lasting impacts on Gaza civilians

Marking three years since its outbreak, the war in Gaza continues to leave widespread displacement and critical humanitarian challenges in its wake, even following the October 2025 ceasefire. Data from the ICRC indicates severe healthcare devastation: out of an initial 34 hospitals, only 19 retained partial operations by the beginning of 2026, while just 3 of the original 8 surgical facilities remained active. Amidst this immense strain, the field hospital in Rafah—run collaboratively by the ICRC, the Palestine Red Crescent Society, and various national societies—provided vital medical support between May 2024 and May 2026, recording upwards of 270,000 patient consultations, 11,900 surgeries, and 1,200 childbirths.

Sylvia Tsang, ICRC Gaza Hospital Programme Manager, detailed the immense operational pressures faced by local medical personnel amidst severe resource shortages. She emphasised the coordination role of the ICRC in aligning international partners, including the HKRC, to optimise medical deployments and resource allocation.

(Right) Sylvia Tsang shared how Gaza field hospitals in Rafah operate and how local medical staff continue delivering services amid limited resources and huge demand.

Stanley Chau, an HKRC medical volunteer deployed to Gaza twice, shared his profound frontline observations and a poignant personal encounter. During his first mission, he treated a patient who had suffered severe blast injuries from a bombing. Astonishingly, when Chau returned for his second deployment, he crossed paths with the very same patient at the hospital, who still required regular follow-up consultations. This reunion deeply moved him, prompting a poignant reflection on how the long-term aftermath of war cannot be easily erased. Having treated patients of all ages, Chau noted that casualties suffer not only from physical wounds but also from prolonged trauma, grief, fractured families, and lost livelihoods, making sustained support encompassing rehabilitation, mental health and psychosocial care, and basic necessities vital.

(Middle) Stanley Chau, who has been deployed to Gaza twice for frontline medical work, shared his experience treating the injured and sick.

Driven by the coordination of the ICRC and the HKRC, local and international medical teams continue to bridge critical gaps. To date, the HKRC has executed 13 medical volunteer deployments totaling 516 days and allocated over HK$2.9 million to support essential water supply, electricity infrastructure, and medical services.

Nepal floods and the imperative of mental health and psychosocial support

Severe monsoon floods and landslides struck Nepal on 26 August 2026, causing widespread devastation. According to the IFRC and the Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS), the disaster claimed 1,453 lives, left 5,179 missing, damaged 7,570 homes, and destroyed critical transport links, severely disrupting community operations and livelihoods.

Having traveled to Nepal in September to coordinate mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) for the flood disaster, Prednison Morales, IFRC Asia Pacific Mental Health and Psychosocial Collaborative Coordinator, highlighted that physical rebuilding must be accompanied by robust mental health interventions. Drawing from his frontline missions, he pointed out that families lost far more than just homes—flash floods washed away their lands, livelihoods, and even centuries of community identity and historical roots, leaving displaced residents grappling with profound insecurity and humiliation in unfamiliar host communities. Furthermore, he cautioned that media and humanitarian actors must avoid portraying affected individuals merely as helpless trauma victims; rather, they should be recognised as resilient survivors whose dignity must be strictly upheld. He emphasised: "Mental health and psychosocial support is an indispensable part of emergency response and should begin alongside the disaster, not only after it has passed. We are training local volunteers in Nepal and supporting them to maintain ongoing contact with affected families in their communities, because psychological trauma and stress do not disappear once relief supplies arrive. Mental health and psychosocial support needs to be integrated into emergency relief and through to medium- and long-term recovery."

Prednison Morales explained how home visits, needs assessments and volunteer training are helping local communities recover step by step.

In response, HKRC allocated approximately HK$1.6 million across two disbursements to procure household kitchen sets, tarpaulins, and essential supplies, alongside activating tracing services and offering mental health and psychosocial support services to the diaspora in Hong Kong.

Alice Ling, Director at the HKRC, who led a delegation to Nepal in mid-October to assess warehouse operations and community recovery, noted that many affected families displaced by past disasters now face renewed displacement. The HKRC is actively exploring cash assistance programmes and integrated medical and water sanitation initiatives to foster sustainable recovery.

(Left) Alice Ling shared how the HKRC works with the Nepal Red Cross Society to plan follow-up humanitarian support and community recovery.

Upholding the seven Fundamental Principles, the HKRC urges the public to remember that humanitarian crises cannot be compared or overlooked, calling for continuous attention and support for vulnerable populations worldwide.

title: Nepal celebrates Bhai Tika, the final day of Tihar - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal celebrates Bhai Tika, the final day of Tihar  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal is celebrating Bhai Tika, the final day of Tihar, with sisters applying ritual tika to their brothers and praying for their long life, good health and prosperity.

Observed every year on the second day of the waxing moon in the Nepali month of Kartik, Bhai Tika is the centrepiece of Tihar, the country’s second-largest festival. Sisters traditionally mark their brothers’ foreheads with tika in five or seven colours. The festival is also known as Yama Dwitiya.

The ritual is reciprocal, with brothers also applying tika to their sisters after receiving it from them. According to Hindu belief, worshipping one’s sisters brings lasting good fortune and prosperity.

Tika can be applied throughout the day, but those seeking an auspicious time have been advised to perform the ritual at 11:07am, said Purushottam Bhattarai, chair of the Nepal Calendar Determination Development Committee. There is no religious restriction on applying tika at other times of the day, he said. However, the committee has said that state officials should observe the ritual at the designated auspicious time.

This year, the committee has advised sisters applying tika to face east and brothers receiving it to face west. This position places the moon, which is in Scorpio, to the right of those receiving tika. The moon will enter Scorpio on Wednesday morning, having been in Libra until then.

Religious scholar Ramchandra Gautam said the same directions could be followed while the moon was in Libra. Hindu scriptures prescribe that the moon should be either in front of or to the right of people during auspicious ceremonies, he said.

full_article:
Press Release

Exchange of Congratulatory Messages between Nepal and the Swiss Confederation

On the occasion of the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Nepal and the Swiss Confederation, congratulatory messages were exchanged between Hon. Mr Shisir Khanal, Minister for Foreign Affairs and H. E. Mr Ignazio Cassis, Federal Councillor of the Swiss Confederation.

Minister Khanal, in his message, extended warm felicitations to the Government and friendly people of Switzerland. He highlighted the longstanding friendship between the two countries, underpinned by cordiality, mutual respect and cooperation, as well as the deepening of bilateral cooperation across multiple areas over the past seven decades. He also expressed deep appreciation for Switzerland’s continued solidarity and assistance to Nepal during times of adversities, including the devastating floods that struck Nepal on 26 August 2026.

Similarly, Federal Councillor Cassis, in his message to Minister Khanal, highlighted the steady growth of Nepal-Switzerland relations over the past 70 years, which have evolved from development cooperation into a broader partnership, encompassing economic relations, democracy and human rights. Fondly recalling his visit to Nepal, he also underscored the strengthening of parliamentary ties between the two countries and expressed hope for the continued growth of bilateral relations in the years ahead.

Nepal and Switzerland established diplomatic relations on 10 November 1956. Both the countries are marking this special occasion by organising various programmes and events throughout the year.

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Singhadurbar, Kathmandu

title: Bhai Tika being observed today, auspicious time set for 11:07 am - The Himalayan Times
description: Bhai Tika being observed today, auspicious time set for 11:07 am  The Himalayan Times

full_article:
KATHMANDU, NOVEMBER 11

Bhai Tika, the final day of the five-day Tihar festival, is being observed across the country today, with the auspicious time for receiving the tika set for 11:07am.

The Nepal Panchanga Nirnayak Development Committee said Bhai Tika can be observed throughout the day, but 11:07am is considered the most auspicious time for those following the prescribed timing. State officials, however, have been advised to receive tika at the auspicious hour.

Bhai Tika is observed on Kartik Shukla Dwitiya, when sisters put multicoloured tika and garlands on their brothers and wish them longevity, good health and prosperity. Brothers subsequently honour their sisters with tika and gifts. The festival is also known as Yama Dwitiya.

This year, sisters giving tika are advised to face east and brothers receiving it to face west so that the Moon in Scorpio remains to the right. The Moon is scheduled to enter Scorpio this morning after remaining in Libra earlier in the day, according to the committee.

On the occasion, sisters worship the lamps, kalash and Ganesh idol established during Laxmi Puja, followed by rituals dedicated to the eight Chiranjeevis and deities including Yama, Yamuna, Dharma Raja and Chitragupta. They then place tika and garlands of makhamali, marigold and chrysanthemum on their brothers and offer traditional foods including walnuts, chestnuts, spices and sel roti. Brothers traditionally give their sisters clothes and cash according to their means.

Bal Gopalashwor temple opens for those without siblings

The Bal Gopalashwor Temple in the middle of Rani Pokhari will be open to devotees who do not have sisters or brothers. The temple is opened only once a year, on Bhai Tika, allowing such devotees to perform worship and receive tika.

Kathmandu Metropolitan City spokesperson Nabin Manandhar said preparations had been completed to open the temple for devotees from Wednesday morning.

The Khangjaneshwor Mahadev Temple at Jayabagishwori also receives devotees without siblings on Bhai Tika. According to cultural expert and Guthi Sansthan chair Dr Govinda Tandan, people without brothers or sisters traditionally gathered at the temple before the Bal Gopalashwor Temple was regularly opened.

The Bal Gopalashwor Temple was regularly opened after 2035 BS. It was damaged in the 2015 earthquake and remained closed for reconstruction until 2020, when it was reopened to devotees.

The Newar community observes the day as Kija Puja. Ritual dates vary according to family traditions, while most Newar communities in Bhaktapur observed Kija Puja on Tuesday following the decision of the priests and astrologers of Taleju Temple.

title: Nepal's Delegation Attends COP 31 in Turkey, Advocates for Climate Justice - Ratopati
description: Nepal's Delegation Attends COP 31 in Turkey, Advocates for Climate Justice  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The UN climate change conference (COP) is currently underway. This conference, being held in Turkey, is the 31st edition of COP. The COP meeting, which began in 1995, is also a common platform for discussing climate change.

Since the convention came into force, this global forum, held annually, has been holding in-depth discussions on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, combating the effects of climate change, and mobilizing financial assistance for least developed and mountainous countries.

Nepal's high-ranking officials are currently in Turkey with the goal of strongly raising their voices for climate justice, compensation, and non-reimbursable grants at this year's conference.

Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Minister for Health and Food Sanitation Nisha Mehta, National Planning Commission Member Prof. Dr. Sanjay Acharya, Secretary of the Ministry of Forest Dr. Rajendra Prasad Mishra, and Member of Parliament Sagar Dhakal are also present there.

What is the Nepali delegation doing at COP-31?

With the fourth day of COP-31 ongoing, members of the Nepali delegation have so far participated in the conference's inaugural plenary session, inaugurated the Nepal Pavilion, attended a high-level side event on mountainous regions, discussed climate finance, and held bilateral meetings.

In various sessions of the conference, the Nepali delegation has drawn the world's attention to the serious impact of climate change on mountainous regions. Foreign Minister Khanal called for ensuring the 1.5-degree Celsius temperature limit in the Himalayan region.

Nepal, like other geographically sensitive and landlocked nations, is experiencing a higher rate of temperature increase than the global average. In the Himalayan region, rapid snowmelt poses a risk of glacial lake outbursts, while in the lower riparian areas, floods, landslides, and droughts in rivers like Bhote Koshi and Trishuli are increasing day by day, he stated.

In addition, Nepal has a schedule of participation in various programs at the conference, which runs until November 20. Today (Wednesday) and tomorrow (Thursday), Foreign Minister Khanal will present Nepal's national stance at the 'Antalya Leaders Summit'. He will also address a high-level event on glaciers and mountain resilience organized by Nepal and four other mountainous countries.

Similarly, Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle is scheduled to participate in half a dozen sessions on climate finance and loss and damage funds by next Sunday. Key political issues will be finalized in the ministerial-level talks on November 17 and 18. Bilateral meetings and regular programs at the Nepal Pavilion will continue throughout the conference, which is scheduled to conclude on November 20.

Nepal's Strong Presence, But No Hope for Achievement

Nepal has suffered damages exceeding 5 billion dollars due to the disaster caused by the Bhote Koshi flood. This disaster has caused severe damage to the livelihoods of local communities, agricultural production, water resources, and valuable infrastructure. The disruption in the mountain ecosystem has added challenges to the water security of the entire region.

It has also been established that the disaster was caused by climate change. In this situation, Nepal is also entitled to climate justice and compensation. Although Nepal has made every effort for this, it does not seem likely to be very fruitful in the current situation. The main reason for this is the indifference shown by large industrial and powerful nations towards compensation.

Powerful Nations Differ on Who Should Pay Compensation

Although the principle that nations with high carbon emissions should pay more compensation has been established, there is currently no consensus between developed and developing countries on how much each should pay.

Specifically, developing and emerging economies argue that developed nations, where industrialization began two to three hundred years ago, should be more responsible for the carbon emissions from that time that have damaged the Earth.

However, developed nations argue that compensation should be determined based on current carbon emissions. If this happens, a large burden will fall on the shoulders of developing nations.

Moreover, some nations, including the United States, are showing reluctance towards compensation. A study by an independent high-level expert group of the United Nations estimates that developing countries will need US$200 to US$400 billion annually for climate-related disaster compensation by 2030. However, only about US$822 million has been committed by 2026.

Besides the Loss and Damage Fund, various international funds have been established for compensation related to climate change. Financial mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund (GCF), the Adaptation Fund (AF), the Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF), and the recently operationalized Loss and Damage Fund are active internationally to combat the effects of climate change. However, due to low budgets, all these funds are not proving effective.

Recently, the Loss and Damage Fund under the United Nations has approved a grant of US$20 million for flood-affected Nepal. However, the amount Nepal is about to receive is very small compared to the total estimated damage.

However, in this situation, there is no possibility of receiving grants as compensation based on climate damage. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle has admitted that it will be difficult to receive even 5-7 billion in grants this year. He stated that the only option now is to pursue concessional loans.

What Should Nepal Do for Climate Justice?

By the time of the 31st edition of COP in Turkey, there is growing skepticism as to whether the commitments made to control the climate crisis will remain limited to speeches and paper documents.

Unless the major carbon-emitting powerful nations show financial generosity, increase non-reimbursable grants, and facilitate technology transfer, global conferences like these are unlikely to yield meaningful results. In this situation, experts say that Nepal needs to think differently.

Climate expert Dr. Kushal Gurung suggests that Nepal should strategically raise its voice for climate compensation, given the reluctance of the world's major polluting nations to provide it. He believes that instead of asking for grants for compensation, Nepal should focus on technical assistance and investment, and for this, bilateral diplomatic efforts should be strengthened.
